frameworks.name: 24 Investing Rules Framework
frameworks.definition: A structured set of decision-making principles for capital deployment, framed as if-then conditional rules that preserve decision-making quality over time.

claims.text: If you can't afford to buy an investment twice, you cannot afford to buy it once; your largest allocation should be no more than 10% of capital, requiring diversity across positions.
claims.speaker: Alex Ramosi
claims.mechanism: Concentration risk: if a single position requires 50% capital, inability to double means overleveraging relative to portfolio resilience.
bounded_by: Does not apply to single-investment businesses (sole proprietor)
Does not apply to illiquid real assets with forced holding periods

claims.text: For any investment or purchase concern (running out of money, loss anxiety), directly purchase insurance rather than avoiding the opportunity; insurance transfers specific risks to third parties at a knowable cost.
claims.speaker: Alex Ramosi
claims.mechanism: Explicit risk transfer: once a specific fear is insurable, avoiding the opportunity becomes irrational—the cost of insurance is known, capping downside.
bounded_by: Does not apply to uninsurable risks (reputation, market demand)
Assumes insurance products are available and affordable

claims.text: When an investment opportunity appears exceptional, immediately seek a second opinion before committing; exceptional-looking deals suggest missing information or misapplied mental models.
claims.speaker: Alex Ramosi
claims.mechanism: Overconfidence bias: optimistic first impressions systematically omit downside scenarios that a disinterested second opinion surfaces.
bounded_by: Does not apply to time-critical decisions where delay destroys deal value

claims.text: Do not invest in a deal until you have articulated all the specific ways capital can be lost; inability to identify loss mechanisms indicates insufficient understanding for capital deployment.
claims.speaker: Alex Ramosi
claims.mechanism: Risk quantification: explicitly modeling failure paths forces internal consistency; deals with identifiable loss vectors are more transparent and survivable than those without.
bounded_by: Does not imply that all loss paths should be preventable
Risk identification does not guarantee capital recovery

claims.text: If you feel pressure to make a decision quickly, pause; rushed deals disproportionately disadvantage the party with incomplete information, which is almost always the new capital provider.
claims.speaker: Alex Ramosi
conditions: External party is applying time pressure
claims.mechanism: Information asymmetry: time pressure reduces due diligence depth; the party imposing urgency already has complete information and high confidence, creating lopsided advantage.
bounded_by: Does not apply when time pressure is mutual (e.g., auction with multiple bidders)

claims.text: Never commit capital if you have only one investment opportunity available; always maintain a portfolio of deal options to force honest comparative evaluation rather than rationalizing a flawed option.
claims.speaker: Alex Ramosi
conditions: multiple opportunities could be available with sufficient effort
claims.mechanism: Comparison bias: a single option is unconsciously rationalized upward when no alternatives exist; the absence of comparison points destroys decision discipline.
bounded_by: Does not apply to forced allocation decisions (capital expiration, regulatory requirement)

claims.text: Distinguish between investing (long-term capital deployment) and trading (short-term position flipping); they require different decision rules, and conflating them is a primary source of investor loss.
claims.speaker: Alex Ramosi
claims.mechanism: Rule mismatch: investing evaluates business fundamentals and long-term compounding; trading evaluates volatility and momentum—applying business logic to trading positions (or vice versa) systematically produces losses.
bounded_by: Does not apply when holding period forces a hybrid approach (e.g., buy-and-hold with tactical adjustments)

claims.text: In any partnership or capital deployment requiring mutual agreement, neither party should move forward unless both explicitly concur; this forces resolution of conflicting models rather than moving ahead with misalignment.
claims.speaker: Alex Ramosi
claims.mechanism: Alignment signaling: unanimous agreement forces articulation of mental models; disagreement reveals different risk assessments or information gaps that must be resolved before execution.
bounded_by: Does not apply to time-critical decisions where consensus-seeking costs the entire opportunity
Requires partners who will not artificially defer to hierarchy

claims.text: Avoid investments or deals that feel cognitively complex or above your comprehension level; lack of understanding is equivalent to gambling, not investing, and eliminates the predictive advantage required for capital deployment.
claims.speaker: Alex Ramosi
claims.mechanism: Epistemic humility: understanding reduces risk because you identify variables and their dependencies; at comprehension threshold you are operating without a mental model, making you equivalent to a random guesser.
bounded_by: Does not imply all investments must be simple
Complexity in execution can be outsourced; complexity in decision logic cannot

claims.text: When you experience fear of missing out (FOMO), treat it as a decision signal to slow down, not accelerate; FOMO is a marker of insufficient analysis and emotional reasoning.
claims.speaker: Alex Ramosi
conditions: Emotional sensation of FOMO arises during decision-making
claims.mechanism: Affect heuristic: FOMO is fear + scarcity + narrative momentum; decisions made under FOMO systematically have weaker due diligence and higher loss rates.

claims.text: Any capital deployment without explicit due diligence (documented information, models, verified data) is not investing; it is unanalyzed bet-making.
claims.speaker: Alex Ramosi
claims.mechanism: Information quality: without documented diligence, you are operating on narrative, hype, or emotional conviction rather than empirical anchors.

claims.text: Invest only in deals where the capital provider receives a business or financial model showing projected growth, value creation, or improvement mechanisms; absence of a model is disqualifying.
claims.speaker: Alex Ramosi
claims.mechanism: Accountability anchoring: a formal model (however crude) creates testable assumptions and forces the proposer to articulate logic rather than relying on charisma.
bounded_by: Does not require prediction accuracy
Does require explicit mathematical structure

claims.text: Judge potential partners and deal-makers primarily on responsiveness speed and expectation-meeting; meticulous response patterns are the earliest signal of operating discipline and execution likelihood.
claims.speaker: Alex Ramosi
conditions: Evaluating a potential business partner or capital recipient
claims.mechanism: Behavioral prediction: how someone handles email commitments predicts how they handle larger commitments; communication discipline is highly correlated with delivery discipline.
bounded_by: Does not account for timezone or communication-style differences
Assumes expectations are set clearly in advance

claims.text: Do not purchase anything that reduces your peace of mind or causes sleep loss; if the psychological cost is high enough to disrupt sleep, the opportunity cost of that stress exceeds financial upside.
claims.speaker: Alex Ramosi
conditions: Investment or purchase decision creates anxiety
claims.mechanism: Cumulative well-being cost: sleep disruption compounds; an investment that causes 1 hour/night stress loss over 2 years costs 730 hours of cognitive function, likely exceeding financial gain.
bounded_by: Does not apply to necessary purchases (housing, education) even if initially stressful

claims.text: Only pursue investments or business decisions that improve personal reputation or brand; neutral moves erode brand by consuming attention without building credibility.
claims.speaker: Alex Ramosi
claims.mechanism: Reputation compounding: each decision either builds or depletes personal brand; neutral decisions have hidden negative cost by occupying mindspace that could build reputation.
bounded_by: Does not apply to foundational investments (health, core relationships)

claims.text: The strongest predictor of future investment performance is past performance; charisma, models, and responsiveness matter, but they do not override track record as the primary signal.
claims.speaker: Alex Ramosi
claims.mechanism: Selection bias control: raw past performance is unfiltered by survivor bias; models and charisma are survivor bias—only showing the successes, not the failures.
bounded_by: Requires sufficient sample size (minimum 3-5 deals, not single outcomes)
Does not discount changing market conditions

claims.text: Once you identify an investment type that has consistently performed well, increase allocation to it rather than diversifying into new investment categories; compounding comes from doing one thing repeatedly, not from variety.
claims.speaker: Alex Ramosi
conditions: Track record of success established in an investment type
claims.mechanism: Skill accumulation compounding: each iteration of a repeated investment type improves pattern recognition and reduces execution error; jumping to new types resets the learning curve.
bounded_by: Does not apply when market conditions change the viability of the proven model

claims.text: Always under-borrow relative to debt capacity; leverage amplifies both returns and losses; over-leveraging compounds into portfolio ruin with high probability over a long enough horizon.
claims.speaker: Alex Ramosi
conditions: Using debt to finance an investment
claims.mechanism: Ruin probability: any position multiplied by zero is still zero; over-leveraging increases the probability of forced liquidation at loss, which eliminates all compounding.
bounded_by: Does not imply zero debt is optimal
Assumes access to debt is available at reasonable rates

claims.text: When someone introduces a deal or proposal with pressure to move quickly, ask clarifying questions and define terms explicitly; inability to articulate the deal structure indicates the proposal is designed to avoid scrutiny.
claims.speaker: Alex Ramosi
claims.mechanism: Clarity as accountability: deals that cannot withstand explicit term definition are typically exploitative or poorly thought-through.

claims.text: Do not enter deals without written contracts specifying expectations, failure scenarios, and remedies; verbal commitments become disputes when circumstances change.
claims.speaker: Alex Ramosi
claims.mechanism: Expectation anchoring: contracts force explicit negotiation of edge cases; the contract-writing process itself surfaces disagreements that would otherwise become costly disputes.

claims.text: Once contracts are executed and terms are set, operate as though the contract does not exist—deliver beyond its requirements, assume good faith, and go offensive in execution; this balances defensive contracting with generous delivery.
claims.speaker: Alex Ramosi
conditions: Contract is finalized and execution phase begins
claims.mechanism: Relationship compounding: defensive legal positioning during execution erodes trust and limits upside; generous execution under clear terms builds loyalty and relationship depth.
bounded_by: Assumes counterparty is operating in good faith

claims.text: In a long-term service relationship with a contractual commitment, mentally model it as a week-to-week engagement; assume the counterparty has no obligation beyond the current period and could leave at any time.
claims.speaker: Alex Ramosi
claims.mechanism: Renewal orientation: treating each period as optional forces delivery quality sufficient to justify renewal; this prevents dependency thinking and keeps execution sharp.

examples.text: Alex Ramosi recounts his early investing experience: he initially thought allocating a third of capital to a single position was appropriate. More experienced investors corrected him, explaining that maximum allocation should be 10% per position, forcing diversification across eight or more opportunities. This ratio (1/10) ensures that no single failure eliminates the portfolio.

When evaluating whether to make an investment, Ramosi checks his emotional state; if fear or anxiety about the decision causes sleep disruption, he rejects it. He reasons that the psychological cost (lost sleep and cognitive function) exceeds financial upside. This applies even to prima-facie good opportunities if they create lingering worry.

In his partnership with Layla, Ramosi notes that she has an impeccable ability to evaluate people, while he tends to be the 'yes man' who sees upside and undersells risk. Their disagreement pattern saves him from mistakes; she will not move forward until they agree, even when he has ultimate decision authority. This veto power only works because she exercises it; a partner who always defers provides no value.

Ramosi describes a due-diligence failure he observed: an investor went forward with a deal based on hype and email pitch alone, without requesting financial models or projections. When the deal failed, the investor had no basis to evaluate whether the failure was predictable or an unforeseeable shock. Absence of a model meant absence of a testable thesis.

practices.text: Ask clarifying questions until you can draw or explain the deal structure back to someone; pretend the person explaining is a listener who doesn't speak English and requires step-by-step explanation.
Always have multiple deal options on the table before committing capital; do not move forward with the only deal available no matter how attractive it appears.
Request written models and financial projections from any capital recipient before evaluating the opportunity; do not proceed with verbal pitch alone.

Track communication responsiveness of partners and deal-makers; if someone says they will respond in two days and they do, that is acceptable; if they miss their own stated timeline, classify it as a disqualifying signal.
When you find an investment type that has worked well multiple times, increase your allocation to it; do not branch into new investment categories.
In partnerships or team decisions, maintain mutual veto power; do not move forward on major decisions unless all parties explicitly agree.
